almost_balanced_bst.title: Hands-on: Build and Rebalance BSTs
almost_balanced_bst.prompt:
Open `structures/bst.c` and implement `bst_build_balanced` and `bst_rebalance`.

Work in two stages:

**Build from a sorted array**
1. Handle the empty range.
2. Choose either valid middle element when a range has even length.
3. Create the root for that range.
4. Recursively build the left and right ranges and set parent links.

**Rebalance an existing BST**
1. Traverse inorder to obtain sorted keys or sorted node references.
2. Rebuild with the midpoint rule.
3. Return a root whose parent is `NULL`.

The harness checks ordering, almost-balance, height, and parent links on odd, even, skewed, and empty inputs. Equivalent linear-time designs pass: lower-middle or upper-middle selection, key copying or node relinking, and different helper names are all valid.
almost_balanced_bst.hint: Use a half-open range `[begin,end)`. Its length is `end-begin`; after choosing `middle`, recurse on `[begin,middle)` and `[middle+1,end)`.

help.concept: Inorder traversal converts BST shape into sorted order. Midpoint recursion converts sorted order into a shape whose left/right subtree sizes differ by at most one.
help.hint_1: For even range lengths, either middle produces valid subtree sizes; stay consistent.
help.hint_2: Pass the newly created root as the `parent` argument for both recursive child calls.

checks.message: Run the provided behavioral harness and use the failing case to locate the logic error.
Equivalent correct implementations are accepted; no exact source phrase is required.

same-bst.title: Which two insertion orders generate the same BST?
same-bst.prompt: Which two insertion orders generate the same BST?
same-bst.hint: Keep the first value as root, then compare the ancestor relationships inside the values below and above that root.

help.concept: Values destined for the left and right subtrees may be interleaved, but each subtree must preserve the relative order that creates the same ancestors.
help.hint_2: Within `{1,2,3}`, value `2` must arrive before `1` and `3`; within `{5,6,7}`, value `6` must arrive before `5` and `7`.

question-3-problem.title: Question 3: Preserve Order While Rebuilding Shape
question-3-problem.bodyMarkdown:
This topic solves all three BST parts with concrete trees and recursive call diagrams.

### Part (a): same elements, different insertion order

Use

```text
A  = (4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7)
A' = (4, 6, 2, 7, 5, 3, 1)
```

Both begin with root `4`. Inside the values below `4`, key `2` arrives before `1` and `3`; inside the values above `4`, key `6` arrives before `5` and `7`. The left- and right-subtree insertions may be interleaved because they do not change each other’s ancestor comparisons.

### Part (b): sorted array to almost-balanced BST

```text
Build(A, left, right, parent):
    if left > right: return NULL
    middle = floor((left + right) / 2)
    root = new Node(A[middle], parent)
    root.left  = Build(A, left, middle - 1, root)
    root.right = Build(A, middle + 1, right, root)
    return root
```

The course implementation uses half-open ranges, but closed ranges, lower middle, and upper middle are all valid when used consistently. Passing indices avoids the extra copying cost of array slices.

### Part (c): arbitrary BST to almost-balanced BST

```text
Rebalance(root):
    nodes = empty array
    StoreInorder(root, nodes)
    return BuildFromSortedNodes(nodes, 0, nodes.length - 1)
```

Inorder traversal recovers sorted order. Midpoint recursion rebuilds the shape. Both phases visit each node once, so the total is `Θ(n)`.

bst-animation.title: Trace Every Insertion and Recursive BST Call
bst-animation.context: **Tree-first explanation:** part (a) inserts each value separately; part (b) grows the actual midpoint-recursion tree for `[1..8]`; part (c) traces recursive inorder collection and a second midpoint-recursion tree.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 1: insert 4
steps.body: 4 becomes the root. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 2: insert 2
steps.body: 2 < 4, so move left and attach 2. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 3: insert 6
steps.body: 6 > 4, so move right and attach 6. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 4: insert 1
steps.body: 1 < 4 and 1 < 2, so attach left of 2. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 5: insert 3
steps.body: 3 < 4 but 3 > 2, so attach right of 2. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 6: insert 5
steps.body: 5 > 4 but 5 < 6, so attach left of 6. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Part (a), insertion 7: insert 7
steps.body: 7 > 4 and 7 > 6, so attach right of 6. The active node and path show the exact comparisons used by `bst_insert`.

steps.title: Trace A' and compare the final ancestor relationships
steps.body: Sequence `A'=(4,6,2,7,5,3,1)` interleaves the two subtrees differently, but `4` is still root, `2` still precedes `1,3`, and `6` still precedes `5,7`. Therefore it produces the same final BST.

steps.title: Part (b): make the root call on [0,8)
steps.body: The range has eight values. Choosing the lower middle gives index `3`, value `4`. The left call receives three values and the right call receives four, so their sizes differ by one.

steps.title: Expand recursion level 1
steps.body: The root call creates two independent recursive calls. `[0,3)` chooses `2`; `[4,8)` chooses `6`. Each call will return one complete child subtree to the waiting parent frame.

steps.title: Expand recursion level 2
steps.body: The next level chooses `1`, `3`, `5`, and `7`. Every node shown is one real non-empty function call. Each empty range below a leaf returns `NULL`.

steps.title: Finish the recursion tree with value 8
steps.body: Range `[6,8)` has two values. With the lower-middle rule it chooses `7`, and its right call `[7,8)` creates `8`. This is still almost balanced because node `7` has subtree sizes `0` and `1`.

steps.title: Return the completed almost-balanced BST
steps.body: Every array value appears exactly once. Sorted positions before each middle become the left subtree, positions after it become the right subtree, and every recursive split differs by at most one node.

steps.title: Count the recursive build work
steps.body: There is one non-empty call per array element. Each call computes one middle index, creates one node, and assigns two pointers—constant local work. Therefore the total is `Θ(n)`; the balanced recursion depth is `Θ(log n)`.

steps.title: Part (c): begin with a right-skewed BST
steps.body: Inserting `1,2,3,4,5,6,7` in sorted order creates a chain. At root `1`, the left subtree has `0` nodes and the right has `6`, so the almost-balanced condition fails immediately.

steps.title: Follow the recursive inorder call chain
steps.body: At each skewed node, the left recursive call returns immediately, the key is appended, and the right recursive call continues to the next node. The call diagram is a chain because the original tree is a chain.

steps.title: Finish inorder with a sorted array
steps.body: BST inorder order is left subtree, current key, right subtree. Because every left key is smaller and every right key is larger, the resulting array is sorted and contains every original key exactly once.

steps.title: Rebuild with a second recursion tree
steps.body: The sorted array is passed to the same midpoint construction. The root call chooses `4`; its child calls choose `2` and `6`; the final calls return leaves `1,3,5,7`.

steps.title: Verify the rebuilt tree
steps.body: The result contains exactly the same keys, remains a valid BST, and now has equal-size subtrees at every internal node. Reusing old nodes or allocating replacement nodes are both valid if keys, ordering, balance, and parent links are correct.

steps.title: Add the two linear phases
steps.body: Inorder traversal processes `n` nodes once. Rebuilding processes the `n` sorted entries once. Therefore `Θ(n)+Θ(n)=Θ(n)`. The array uses `Θ(n)` extra space; a skewed traversal can use `Θ(n)` call-stack space.
